views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Follow through on the announced Section 301 tariffs — release the final ~$50B, 25% list as scheduled — to preserve the credibility and leverage we have built, but signal clearly and publicly that the door remains open to a negotiated settlement (increased US purchases, structural commitments on tech transfer) once China engages seriously. Do not broaden scope or add new non-tariff actions that would over-extend the confrontation, and keep the ZTE reconciliation channel alive to avoid alienating the business community and spurring Congressional backlash.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: From the US vantage this is a leverage position, not a defensive one. We initiated the Section 301 investigation (Aug 2017) and have steadily escalated: steel/aluminum tariffs (Mar 8), a ~$50B/1,300-line proposed tariff list targeting China's tech and 'Made in China 2025' sectors (Apr 3), and a non-tariff ZTE denial order (Apr 16). The May 19 joint statement where China agreed to 'significantly increase' US purchases showed the opponent is amenable, and the May 29 decision to proceed with 25% tariffs on ~$50B reasserted our leverage after the truce collapsed. The macro backdrop favors us: the broad dollar at ~112 (multi-year high), 10-yr at ~2.98%, consumer sentiment ~98, industrial production rising — the US economy is strong enough to absorb the disruption, while the persistent ~$30.8B monthly goods deficit with China (April, BEA) is the structural card we are playing. Offsetting risks that temper the reading: China's proposed retaliation on ~$50B including soybeans and autos threatens the politically sensitive farm belt and could raise consumer/input prices (economists already warn tariffs raise prices and destroy jobs), and Congressional pushback on the ZTE accommodation complicates a broad strategy. Hence this is a mild opportunity (~-0.35), not a clear one: we have leverage and domestic political tailwind from being tough on China, but retaliation and farm-belt/price exposure argue against maximal escalation. The action stance (~-0.45) rises to the announced tariff step as leverage, but stops short of a wider non-tariff campaign to keep a negotiated exit available and limit second-order damage.
key_factors: US initiated and dominates the escalation sequence (301, 232 steel/aluminum, ZTE denial order)
US macro strength: dollar ~112, 10yr ~2.98%, sentiment ~98, IP rising
Persistent ~$30.8B monthly goods deficit with China is the structural leverage
China agreed to increase US purchases (May 19) before truce collapsed (May 29)
Countervailing risks: China's proposed retaliation on soybeans/autos (farm belt), consumer price risk, Congressional backlash on ZTE
threat_score=score=-0.35 (opportunity/leverage, tempered by retaliation and price risk); action_score=-0.45 (escalate as leverage, not maximal)
